claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by the interplay between rapid thermal processing and localized atomic interactions during nucleation.
Modulating heating kinetics changes the balance between stochastic atomic deposition and thermodynamically driven phase separation.
Controlled heating kinetics can favor formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Changing the heating rate and precursor delivery scheme modulates nucleation dynamics.
Localized atomic-arrangement dynamics during nanoparticle nucleation mediate the balance between atomic mixing and segregation.
Localized atomic-arrangement dynamics during nucleation can be revealed by in situ spectroscopic signals.
Adjusting the heating rate changes the energy barriers for atomic diffusion and nucleation.
Adjusting the heating rate changes the timescales of atomic diffusion and nucleation.
Controlling diffusion and nucleation parameters enables kinetic trapping of the constituent atoms in a homogeneous solid solution.
Deviations from the optimal heating profile promote phase separation.
Deviations from the optimal heating profile promote elemental segregation.
Deviations from the optimal heating profile promote uncontrolled particle morphology.
An optimized heating profile and precursor-delivery schedule will improve single-phase solid-solution characteristics relative to conventional rapid heating and cooling.
An optimized heating profile and precursor-delivery schedule will reduce phase separation and elemental segregation relative to the baseline.
Spectroscopic-signature changes under the optimized conditions will indicate more uniform nucleation and agree with the stochastic model.
Conventional rapid heating and cooling produces uncontrolled crystal structures with phase separation and elemental segregation in the stated baseline.
The proposed behavior applies to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
The proposed behavior applies within processing regimes near the thermal-decomposition threshold.
The predicted behavior may not hold at substantially lower or higher temperatures.
The predicted behavior may not hold for nanoparticles containing five or fewer elements.
